content: Endemic countries are encouraged to implement strategies that combine vector control for malaria with efforts to eliminate lymphatic filariasis (LF) as a public health issue. These strategies should also address specific technical challenges. Albendazole monotherapy for mass drug administration (MDA) in LF elimination is recommended in areas co-endemic with loiasis where ivermectin has not been previously introduced, regardless of the presence of onchocerciasis. In regions where ivermectin MDA has been used for LF or onchocerciasis elimination, the ivermectin-albendazole (IA) regimen can continue under current guidelines for onchocerciasis management in loiasis co-endemic areas. There are no direct comparative studies evaluating the effectiveness of biannual versus annual albendazole MDA. Studies on annual albendazole administration alone have shown inconsistent results. Limited observational evidence suggests that biannual albendazole MDA is both safe and effective, though the quality of this evidence is very low. There are no equity concerns between biannual and annual albendazole MDA, and biannual treatment may improve access for populations unable to participate in a single annual round. Biannual albendazole is already being implemented in some LF and loiasis co-endemic countries, demonstrating its feasibility and acceptability among stakeholders. However, the short-term resource requirements for biannual MDA are expected to increase due to the need for two rounds per year instead of one. Certain populations are excluded from biannual albendazole MDA based on existing WHO guidelines. These include pregnant women in their first trimester, individuals with a history of neurocysticercosis or seizures, and children under two years of age. WHO recommends biannual albendazole MDA over annual administration in implementation units (IUs) where LF is co-endemic with loiasis and ivermectin has not been distributed for LF or onchocerciasis. This is a conditional recommendation due to the very low quality of evidence, pending new data and updated WHO guidelines. Monitoring and evaluation should follow WHO guidance, including establishing baseline endemicity through mapping or sentinel site surveys before starting MDA, conducting coverage evaluations after initial rounds, and monitoring mid-term and long-term impacts at sentinel and spot-check sites. If epidemiological thresholds (e.g., <1% microfilaremia or <2% antigenemia) are not met, additional MDA rounds are required before reassessment. The evidence for the effectiveness of biannual albendazole MDA is limited. One observational study showed a 3% reduction in microfilaremia prevalence and an 8% reduction in circulating filarial antigen prevalence after 36 months of biannual albendazole treatment. These findings were indirectly compared to studies on annual albendazole, which showed minimal clearance of microfilariae or antigen. Safety data from the WHO International Drug Monitoring Programme indicate no unknown adverse reactions to albendazole, with the most common side effects being vomiting, headache, abdominal pain, pruritus, nausea, diarrhea, and rash. The balance of benefits and risks likely favors biannual albendazole MDA, though the overall quality of evidence remains very low. No studies have assessed the cost-effectiveness or impact on health equity of biannual versus annual albendazole MDA. However, biannual treatment may increase the likelihood of individuals receiving at least one dose per year. Implementation of biannual albendazole MDA has been shown to be feasible in some countries, with routine administration to school-aged children for soil-transmitted helminth control providing a model for its use. WHO will support countries in adapting and implementing these guidelines, integrating them into national health systems, and addressing barriers to implementation. WHO will monitor the impact of these guidelines by collecting data on the number of countries and IUs adopting alternative MDA regimens, as well as progress toward LF elimination criteria. Data will be reviewed annually, and updates to the guidelines may be issued as new evidence becomes available. This approach aligns with the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) framework and supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by addressing poverty, health, education, gender equality, economic growth, and inequality reduction.
